summary: Specifies RSVP-TE extensions for Lock Instruct and Loopback in GMPLS-controlled label switched paths. Lock Instruct lets an operator take a path out of service gracefully, while Loopback sends traffic back for testing.

eli5.summary: Two controls for a road: close it for repair, or turn traffic around for testing.

questions: what is the rsvp-te loopback attribute flag
subtitle: RSVP-TE signaling to lock a GMPLS label switched path and loop traffic back at a chosen node for testing.

tldr.problem: Operators of GMPLS-controlled networks need on-demand Lock Instruct and Loopback functions to take a path out of service and test it, and want one signaling approach for all the technologies involved.
tldr.mechanism: Lock uses the A (Administratively down) bit of the ADMIN_STATUS object, while loopback uses a new Loopback bit (bit 13) in the Attribute Flags TLV, addressed to a node through the ERO Hop Attributes subobject.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the Path and Resv procedures, four new error sub-codes (26 to 29) under the OAM Problem error code, and the IANA assignments needed.

today: RFC 7571 is a Proposed Standard. It has not been obsoleted and no later RFC is recorded as updating it.

sections.title: Lock Instruct and Loopback
sections.content:
The requirements for Lock Instruct (LI) and Loopback (LB) in the MPLS Transport Profile are in RFC 5860, and their framework is in RFC 6371. A Label Switched Path (LSP) that is locked is prevented from carrying user data traffic. Loopback can only be applied to an LSP that was previously locked.

LI and LB are OAM (Operations, Administration, and Maintenance) functions useful for technologies that use Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) as the control plane, such as time-division multiplexing, wavelength-division multiplexing and packet switching. This RFC extends RSVP-TE so that one approach provisions them all. RFC 7487 covers proactive OAM functions, but not on-demand ones like LI and LB. For MPLS-TP networks, this document complements RFC 6435.
sections.eli5: Operators sometimes need to close a path and then test it. This document says how the routers along the path are told to do that.

sections.title: Flags Used for Lock and Loopback
sections.content:
Lock status reuses the A (Administratively down) bit in the Administrative Status (ADMIN_STATUS) object from RFC 3471 and RFC 3473.

Loopback needs a new Loopback flag in the Attribute Flags TLV from RFC 5420. It says that a particular node on the LSP must enter loopback mode, and can also report that node's loopback state. It is bit number 13, carried in Path messages (yes), not in Resv messages (no), and carried in the Record Route Object (RRO) Attributes subobject (yes).
sections.eli5: Lock is a switch that already existed. Loopback needed a brand new switch, so the document adds one.

sections.title: Locking and Unlocking an LSP
sections.content:
To lock an LSP, the ingress node MUST send a Path message with the A bit set and the Reflect (R) bit in ADMIN_STATUS set. The egress node SHOULD try to take the LSP out of service. On success it MUST send a Resv message with the A bit set. Otherwise it MUST send a PathErr with Error Code OAM Problem and the new Error Value Lock Failure, and following Resv messages MUST have the A bit cleared. While the LSP is locked, later Path and Resv messages MUST keep the A bit set.

Unlocking mirrors this. The ingress sends a Path message with the A bit cleared, and the egress SHOULD try to restore service. On success it MUST send a Resv with the A bit cleared. On failure it MUST send a PathErr with Unlock Failure, and following Resv messages MUST have the A bit set.
sections.eli5: The first router says 'close this road'. The last router answers 'done' or 'I could not'. Opening the road again works the same way in reverse.

sections.title: Putting a Node into Loopback
sections.content:
A loopback request can go to the egress node or to a particular intermediate node, which is addressed using the mechanism of RFC 7570. The ingress node MUST ensure the LSP is already locked before requesting loopback. It sends a Path message with the Loopback flag set, keeps the A bit set, and MUST make sure the intended entity is explicitly identified by the ERO subobject immediately before the ERO Hop Attributes subobject.

The target node checks that the A bit is set; if not, it MUST ignore the request. It then checks that the ERO subobject type is less than 32, and that type 1 (IPv4 prefix) has prefix length 32 and type 2 (IPv6 prefix) has prefix length 128. If the entity is not explicitly identified, the request is ignored and a Bad EXPLICIT_ROUTE object error SHOULD be generated. Otherwise the node SHOULD try to enter loopback on that entity. If that subobject is a label subobject, loopback applies to the direction given by its U bit.

On success the node sets the Loopback flag when it adds an RRO Hop Attributes subobject, and the A bit stays set. On failure it MUST send a PathErr with OAM Problem and the new value Loopback Failure.
sections.eli5: Before turning cars around at one spot, the road must be closed. The chosen spot checks that it really is closed and that it was named clearly, then it does the turnaround.

sections.title: Leaving Loopback and Unlocking
sections.content:
To end loopback, the ingress sends a Path message with the Loopback flag cleared, still keeping the A bit set. The target node SHOULD try to leave loopback. On success it MUST clear the flag in the RRO Hop Attributes subobject and push that subobject onto the RRO. Otherwise it MUST send a PathErr with Exit Loopback Failure.

Only after loopback is cleared may the ingress node remove the lock. It MUST NOT request to exit lock mode while the LSP is still in loopback, and the egress node MUST ignore such a request.
sections.eli5: You first stop turning cars around, and only then open the road again. Opening it too early is not allowed.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content:
IANA assigned bit 13, named Loopback, in the Attribute Flags sub-registry. For Path messages the value is yes, for Resv no, and it is allowed in the RRO and ERO.

It also assigned four Error Value sub-codes under the OAM Problem error code: 26 (Lock Failure), 27 (Unlock Failure), 28 (Loopback Failure) and 29 (Exit Loopback Failure). Finally, the allocation rule for Explicit Route Object subobject types 5 to 31 now reads Unassigned, for explicit resource identification.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers was updated so everyone uses the same numbers for these new signals and errors.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it introduces no new security issues beyond those in RFC 3209, RFC 3473 and RFC 7570, and points to RFC 5920 for a broader discussion of GMPLS security.

It adds one privacy note: reporting loopback status in the RRO may reveal details about a node that the operator wants to keep confidential. The privacy considerations in paragraph 3 of Section 5 of RFC 7570 also apply.
sections.eli5: Telling everyone which spot is being tested might give away secrets, so operators should be careful what they share.

items.label: Unlock Failure
items.desc: Egress could not unlock the LSP.

items.label: Loopback Failure
items.desc: Node could not enter loopback mode.

items.label: Exit Loopback Failure
items.desc: Node could not leave loopback mode.
